# **Overview**

Users have been reporting some pretty bad performance problems lately. We need a
solid way to test the app before releasing new code to fix these and make sure
they don't come back. Here are the main issues users are running into:

- **Memory Crashes:** The application simply runs out of memory and crashes
  (Out-of-Memory or OOM errors), especially when processing large amounts of
  data like huge base64 image files.
- **UI Flickering and High CPU:** The Gemini CLI uses a framework called React
  Ink. This framework completely redraws the whole terminal screen every time
  something changes. This can cause CPU usage to spike over 100% and makes the
  screen flicker.
- **Extremely Slow Startups:** Sometimes the CLI takes up to 18 minutes just to
  start. This happens because the system gets stuck reading multiple SKILL.md
  files one by one over slow network connections.
- **Long Delays and "Ghosting":** Users see long "Thinking..." pauses. Also, a
  bug sometimes keeps that thinking message on the screen even after the model
  is done responding.

![][image2]  
\[Current Architectural bottle neck in the terminal rendering pipeline\]

# **Current Test harness**

**What the Tests Target:** The main goal for these performance tests is to
automatically stop bad code from being merged. To be as accurate as possible, we
run the entire Gemini CLI from start to finish. We don't just test small parts.
Network speeds and APIs can be inconsistent, so we use a "mock" model instead of
calling the real Gemini backend. We also run these tests on Windows, macOS, and
Linux to catch bugs specific to those systems.

**Is the Current Harness Fully Capable?:** Right now, about half of the
performance testing work is done. The harness can run basic tests. It detects
CPU issues and filters out background server noise. It can also force memory
cleanups to find leaks. However, since the project isn't finished, the harness
can't handle every testing scenario yet.

To stop these bugs from reaching users, the team is building new automated tests
to catch them early:

- **Memory Tests (npm run test:memory):** These tests look for memory leaks.
  They force the system to clean up memory and then check what's left. This
  ensures no extra data is clogging up the system.
- **CPU Tests (npm run test:perf):** These check how fast the code is and how
  much power it uses. They use math to ignore lag from the testing servers. This
  means we don't blame the code for a slow server.

**The Problem:** Currently, developers set the target scores by running tests on
their own fast laptops. When the automated tests run on slower cloud servers,
they fail because they can't keep up with those laptop speeds.

Before we can add a variety of tests that alert on performance and memory issues
for various scenarios using this test harness \- we need to be able to set
baselines in a reliable manner across platforms and configurations of terminal
buffers etc.

# **Approaches for Setting Baselines**

To fix this baseline mismatch, there are two main approaches we can take:

**Approach A: Normalize for the Testing Servers (Configuration Matrices)**

- **How it works:** We run the tests directly on the automated cloud servers and
  record _those_ scores as the official, static baselines.
- **Pros:** We get an absolute standard. We can always track exactly how fast
  the app is compared to a specific date in the past.
- **Pros/ Cons:** If the cloud provider quietly upgrades or changes their server
  hardware, all of our baselines become instantly outdated and trigger false
  alarms, requiring a massive effort to reset everything. This is also a pro as
  any updates to the servers is something that we must be aware of anyway to
  understand how it may regress or may reset the perf/mem numbers.

**Approach B: Machine-Agnostic Daily Comparisons**

- **How it works:** We stop using saved baseline files. Instead, every night, we
  run the test on _today's_ code and _yesterday's_ code on the exact same
  server, and compare the two against each other.
- **Pros:** Hardware differences no longer matter. Because both tests run on the
  exact same machine at the same time, we only measure the actual impact of the
  code changes made that day.
- **Cons:** It introduces the "Boiling Frog" vulnerability.

![][image3]

# **Recommended Strategy: Github Action \+ Approach A**

We need to ensure that developers are able to find a quick way to integrate
performance tests to be run by github actions or via a \`/run perf\` or \`/run
mem\` command in the PR page to have a report of performance and/or memory tests
comparing results between current main and the PR we intend to merge to main.
This is a convenient way for a developer to check how their PR may positively or
negatively affect the performance and memory of GCLI.

If a PR necessitates a change in the baseline configuration we need a way to
ensure that PR merge also triggers an update baseline action. This is so that
the future runs on the nightly is comparing against the new baselines updated
for that day.

We also need to ensure that the report is human readable. For example instead of
reporting a large number of bytes leaked due to the PR – reporting it in terms
of MB etc.

**When to Run What:**

- **For per PR Checks (Pull Requests):** We must have set up a way to run the
  perf and memory tests via the PR on the github server and also on the local
  machines (such as npm run perf \- when run locally should trigger a comparison
  of the numbers for the updated main branch versus the current branch where the
  work is being tested.
- **For Nightly Build Health (Daily Audits): Use Approach A.** We must run
  strict tests on a dedicated set of servers for each platform each day. This
  stops the "boiling frog" problem where performance slowly gets worse over
  time. It acts as an anchor to make sure the app hasn't slowed down from many
  tiny changes.

The trigger to update the baselines has to come via a PR merge after approval
from a specific group of people (like ask-mode approvers \- we can probably have
a perf-approvers list)

**Why this works:**  
.  
Local runs lets developers move fast without worrying about server hardware
during PR checks. Approach A is the safety net. It runs on fixed hardware to
keep the app's core performance within acceptable limits.
